title: What Does Booking Offer That Hilton Does Not?
detail:
What Does Booking Offer That Hilton Does Not?

Hilton Worldwide (HLT) and Booking Holdings both make money when travelers fill hotel rooms, but the companies measure their business differently. Hilton collects management and franchise fees from hotel owners using its brands. Booking measures growth by the number of room nights travelers reserve through platforms like Booking.com. Investors pay 51.5 times earnings for Hilton, compared with 17.5 for Booking, suggesting the market favors the Hilton model. So what does Booking offer that Hilton does not, and what does Hilton have to keep doing to be worth that much more?

Hilton Is Still Adding Hotels As Promised

Hilton must continue expanding the number of properties in its system, and so far the company is maintaining that pace. Net units increased 6.1% in fiscal Q2 2026. Management said on the July 28, 2026 call that Hilton can deliver 6% to 7% growth for the foreseeable future, adding that most properties expected to open in 2026 are already under construction.

During the same call, management raised the company's 2026 forecast for growth in revenue per available room, the hotel industry's measure of room income, to 3% to 3.5%.

Booking Holdings brought a different kind of news on its August 4, 2026 call. Management said the expectation for gross bookings was lower than before, mainly because of slower flight ticket growth, while the outlook for accommodation remained largely unchanged. Hilton's update was a raise about rooms, and Booking's cut was about flights.

Hilton Charges Owners Less And Has Less Cash

Hilton also faces the challenge of growing profits while reducing the fees it charges hotel owners, a balance the company has yet to demonstrate. Management lowered the loyalty fees charged to most hotels, citing the growing scale of Hilton Honors. The company also trimmed its 2026 net income forecast to $1.9 billion at the midpoint, down from $1.92 billion in April.

Hilton also operates with less cash backing its borrowing. Debt minus cash stood at $13.0 billion at June 30, 2026, compared with $3.48 billion for Booking, whose cash covers most of its debt.

How Hilton And Booking Compare On Growth And Margin

Hilton investors are not paying a higher multiple for faster growth or wider margins, as Booking leads in both categories. Booking grew revenue by 12.9% over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, while Hilton posted 8.7% growth. Booking has also expanded faster on average, growing 13.5% a year over the last three years, compared with 8.6% for Hilton.

title: Airbnb vs. Booking: Which Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
detail:
Airbnb vs. Booking: Which Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Sara Appino, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 21, 2026 at 4:23 AM MST 6 min read
ABNB
BKNG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The global travel landscape is shifting, leaving investors to choose between two dominant forces. Should you favor the unique inventory of Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) or the massive scale of Booking Holdings (NASDAQ:BKNG)?

Airbnb specializes in individual home listings and unique experiences, while Booking operates a diverse ecosystem including Booking.com and OpenTable. Both companies dominate the travel industry, providing essential infrastructure for global vacationers. Comparing their business models and financial health helps clarify which fits your long-term investment strategy.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb is a global marketplace for stays and experiences. The company is a prominent name among travel and tourism stocks, connecting over 5 million hosts with guests across 220 countries. Its platform features over 9 million active listings, and it relies on a network of third-party service providers for the vast majority of its critical community support operations.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $12.3 billion, representing growth of approximately 10.8% compared to the previous year. The company reported net income of close to $2.5 billion for the period, a figure slightly lower than the $2.6 billion reported in FY 2024. This performance resulted in a net margin of roughly 20.4%, illustrating how much of each sales dollar the company retains as profit after all expenses.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.3x, a metric measuring total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, was nearly 1.4x, suggesting the company has sufficient resources for short-term needs. Free cash flow reached roughly $4.6 billion, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Booking

With diverse brands including Booking.com, Agoda, and OpenTable, the company derives its revenue from consumers and partners, relying on third-party travel service providers and search platforms for its inventory and traffic. It operates in more than 220 countries and territories and managed about 4.7 million accommodation properties as of mid-2026.

For FY 2025, revenue reached close to $26.9 billion, a growth of roughly 13.4% over the $23.7 billion generated in FY 2024. The company generated net income of approximately $5.4 billion, which contributed to a net margin of nearly 20.1% for the fiscal period. These results demonstrate the company's ability to maintain high levels of revenue while capturing a significant share of the global travel market.

title: What Changed In Airbnb's Story?
detail:
What Changed In Airbnb's Story?

Airbnb (ABNB) stock trades at 38.6 times earnings, against 22.9 for the S&P 500. Shareholders paying that much need to know what they are buying, but there is a twist: what management talks up on its calls has changed. During the fiscal Q3 2024 call, management said it was focused on making hosting just as popular as traveling on Airbnb, which means getting more people to rent out their homes. On the latest call, management made the case for something else. So what is it?

Airbnb Now Puts Hotels In The Spotlight

During the fiscal Q2 2026 call in August, management highlighted hotels, saying hotel nights are growing about three times faster than the homes business. The company also described the next stage for Airbnb as a one-stop shop for travel, and said it had expanded Airbnb Services into grocery delivery, car rental, airport pickup and luggage storage.

Before that, hosts were the supply story. Management introduced co-host networks on the fiscal Q3 2024 call as an easy way for a homeowner to find a local host to run the listing. By the fiscal Q2 2025 call, management said 100,000 listings were managed by co-hosts and that the program could lead to millions more homes on Airbnb. Co-hosts did not come up on the latest call, and hotels took the spotlight. Homes still got attention: management said more than 150,000 homes in World Cup host cities were listed on Airbnb for the first time.

How Big Are Hotels Next To Airbnb's Homes?

Hotels still represent a small part of Airbnb. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that they account for a single-digit percentage of nights booked. As a result, homes still make up the great bulk of what guests book, even with hotel nights growing about three times as fast.

Management said nights and seats booked grew 10% from a year earlier, accelerating from fiscal Q1 2026. Revenue grew 16.5% in fiscal Q2 2026, faster than the 12.7% growth in fiscal Q2 2025.

Should Airbnb Holders Worry About Its Push Into Hotels?

So far the push reads as more reassuring than concerning, because Airbnb as a whole is growing faster, not slower. Revenue over the twelve months to June 2026 grew 13.6%, against 10.2% for the twelve months before. Management also said roughly 35% of first-time hotel guests return to Airbnb to book a home, meaning hotels appear to be bringing new guests to the homes side.

The concern is not hotels, but the supply of homes. In September, the EU set out plans to give European cities more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb. On the August call, before those plans came out, management said policy is a risk, but not an existential one.

Shares of Booking Holdings (BKNG) have lost 17.2% over the past year, lagging the S&P 500 and its 17.4% return. Following that decline, the stock trades at 17.3 times earnings. That multiple sits below the company's average of 28.3 over its last 12 fiscal quarter ends. A lower P/E means paying less for each dollar of profit, but that discount only pays off if the profit keeps growing. So what would have to go right for Booking Holdings stock to climb from here?

Booking Holdings Would Gain Most From Selling More Travel

Selling more travel would generate most of the stock's potential gain. Under Trefis's three-year scenario, higher revenue accounts for 82.4% of the upside. That means more room nights, the nights travelers book through platforms like Booking.com, alongside more flight and attraction tickets. Following these assumptions, the stock would appreciate about 49% in three years, excluding dividends.

An expanding multiple provides a further 28.4% of the upside, assuming a higher P/E, while a lower margin takes 10.8% back. This scenario lifts the P/E from 17.3 to 19.4. Even after that increase, the multiple would remain below the stock's own 12-quarter average of 28.3.

Where Booking Holdings' Sales Growth Comes From

The scenario models revenue growth of 11.6% a year. That pace falls slightly behind the 12.9% Booking Holdings delivered over the twelve months to fiscal Q2 2026. Growth slowed in the latest quarter, so the scenario needs the pace to pick up again as travelers book more nights and more of the rest of their trips through the company's sites. Room nights increased 5% and revenue rose 8% in fiscal Q2 2026, management said on the August 4, 2026 call. Executives issued a slower guide for the following period, forecasting fiscal Q3 2026 revenue growth of 4% to 6%. However, that guidance covers a single quarter rather than three years, and it assumes the conflict in the Middle East keeps weighing on long-haul travel.

Booking Holdings is also capturing more business from its most loyal customers. Members of its Genius levels 2 and 3 accounted for more than 30% of active customers in fiscal Q2 2026, representing an increase from a year earlier. Management also said that trips combining several bookings grew more than twice as fast as total transactions at Booking.com.

title: Up 10% in the Last Two Weeks, Is Airbnb the Perfect Stock for Today's Market?

Up 10% in the Last Two Weeks, Is Airbnb the Perfect Stock for Today's Market?

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) has mostly been a disappointment for investors after initially surging out of the gate in its 2020 IPO, but in 2026, the stock is finally gaining momentum.

The #1 home-sharing platform has delivered better-than-expected growth, solid margins, and it's leveraging AI to improve user satisfaction. Meanwhile, it is expanding its platform with expanded experiences and guest services offerings.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Over the last two weeks, the stock is up 9.4%, even as the S&P 500 has fallen 1.6%, as the chart below shows.

ABNB data by YCharts

Airbnb's gains have come as the tech sector has tumbled on concerns about an AI bubble and rising interest rates. However, the company has demonstrated its resilience and is well-positioned to thrive in such an environment. Here are three reasons why Airbnb is poised to be a winner in today's stock market.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. It wins on high interest rates

Stock investors generally dislike rising interest rates. After all, higher interest rates tend to make the bond market more attractive, leading investors to rotate out of stocks and into bonds. Additionally, higher interest rates put pressure on high-priced stocks like much of the tech sector, as it makes future earnings less valuable due to a higher discount rate in the discounted cash flow.

Normally, a company like Airbnb would be susceptible to that pressure, but the home-sharing leader actually earns significant profit from interest income thanks to the funds it holds in between customer bookings and disbursement. Through the first half of the year, it's earned $363 million in interest income, more than a third of its before-tax profit, and that number is likely to go up as interest rates go up. As of the end of the second quarter, the company held $12.2 billion in "funds receivable and amounts held on behalf of customers," on which it earns interest. That's a substantial advantage of its business model and gives it resilience when many of its tech stock peers are falling in the face of higher interest rates.

2. It won't be disrupted by agentic AI

The launch of Meta Platforms' Muse also exposed a hidden advantage of Airbnb. Unlike its online travel agency (OTA) rivals Expedia and Booking, Airbnb's inventory is mostly specific to its platform. Expedia and Booking, on the other hand, are essentially middlemen, connecting users to hotels and acting as a clearinghouse for hotels that want to get their listings in front of prospective customers.
